sach.title: Why Sleep Helps You Remember
sach.text: Sleep is not simply a pause in the day. While you rest, your brain is busy sorting what happened while you were awake. During deep sleep, a region called the hippocampus replays recent experiences, and these patterns are gradually transferred to the cortex, where long-term memories are stored. Researchers have observed this replay in animals: rats that learned a maze showed the same sequence of brain activity again while they slept. In people, studies have found that those who sleep after learning new words or facts usually remember them better the next day than those who stay awake for the same amount of time. Sleep also seems to help the brain decide what to keep and what to forget. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam may therefore backfire: you gain hours of study but lose the process that helps the material stick.

Dreams predict what will happen the next day

sach.title: The Octopus
sach.text: The octopus is one of the most unusual animals in the sea. It has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, while the third sends it around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, because it uses a copper-based molecule to carry oxygen instead of the iron-based one found in human blood. Even more surprising is its nervous system. An octopus has around 500 million neurons, and about two thirds of them are located in its arms rather than its brain. Each arm can taste and touch, and can react partly on its own. Octopuses are also skilled problem solvers. In experiments, they have learned to open jars, escape from tanks and recognise individual people. Many species can change the colour and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second, which helps them hide from predators or surprise their prey.

sach.title: How GPS Finds You
sach.text: Every time a phone shows your position on a map, it relies on signals from space. The Global Positioning System, or GPS, is run by the United States and uses around thirty satellites orbiting about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. Each satellite constantly sends out a signal that contains its position and the exact time it was sent. A receiver on the ground compares these times with its own clock. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, the tiny delay reveals how far away each satellite is. With signals from at least four satellites, the receiver can calculate its location, usually to within a few metres. The timing has to be extremely precise, so the satellites carry atomic clocks. Engineers even have to correct for effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity, which make clocks in orbit run at a slightly different rate.

sach.title: Why Honey Lasts
sach.text: Honey is one of the few foods that hardly ever goes bad. Archaeologists have reported finding pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were thousands of years old and still had not spoiled. The secret lies in its chemistry. Honey contains very little water and a great deal of sugar, which draws moisture out of any bacteria or fungi that land in it, so they cannot survive. It is also fairly acidic. In addition, bees add an enzyme to the nectar that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a natural disinfectant. To make a single jar of honey, bees must visit an enormous number of flowers. Honey that turns solid has not gone off; it has simply crystallised. Gently warming the jar in a bowl of hot water will make it runny again. The best way to keep honey fresh is to close the lid tightly, because honey slowly absorbs water from the air.

sach.title: The First Telescopes
sach.text: The telescope was not invented by a famous scientist but by spectacle makers. In 1608, Hans Lipperhey, a lens maker in the Netherlands, applied for a patent on a tube with two lenses that made distant objects appear closer. News of the device spread quickly across Europe. In Italy, Galileo Galilei heard about it and built his own improved version in 1609. Instead of looking at ships or armies, he pointed it at the night sky. What he saw changed astronomy forever. He discovered mountains and craters on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way and, in January 1610, four moons circling Jupiter. These moons showed that not everything in the sky revolves around the Earth. Today the four largest moons of Jupiter are still called the Galilean moons, in his honour.
gist: How the telescope was invented and changed astronomy
How glasses are made
Why Jupiter is the largest planet

sach.title: How Tides Work
sach.text: Twice a day, the sea along many coasts rises and falls. These movements, called tides, are caused mainly by the Moon. Its gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans, creating a bulge of water on the side facing the Moon. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth. As the Earth rotates, most places pass through both bulges, which is why there are usually two high tides and two low tides each day. Because the Moon also moves along its orbit, high tide comes about fifty minutes later each day. The Sun plays a role too. When the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, at full moon and new moon, their effects combine and produce especially strong tides, known as spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the difference between high and low water can reach about sixteen metres.

How to surf big ocean waves
Why the ocean is salty
q: About how much later does high tide come each day?

sach.title: Emperor Penguins
sach.text: Penguins are birds that cannot fly, but they are superb swimmers. Their wings have evolved into stiff flippers that push them through the water, and some species can dive hundreds of metres deep. Almost all penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere. Only the Galápagos penguin occasionally crosses the equator. The largest species, the emperor penguin, breeds on the sea ice of Antarctica during the dark, freezing winter. After the female lays a single egg, she passes it to the male and walks back to the sea to feed. For about two months, the male balances the egg on his feet under a warm fold of skin, eating nothing at all. Thousands of males huddle together against the wind, slowly taking turns at the cold edge of the group. When the chick hatches, the female returns and the parents take turns caring for it.

sach.title: Bamboo
sach.text: Bamboo looks like a tree, but it is actually a giant grass. Some species are among the fastest-growing plants in the world and can grow close to a metre in a single day under ideal conditions. Unlike trees, a bamboo stem does not get thicker over the years. It reaches its full width when it first shoots out of the ground and then simply grows taller. Bamboo is extremely strong for its weight, which is why it has been used for centuries in Asia to build houses, bridges and scaffolding. Even today, construction workers in Hong Kong put up bamboo scaffolding around tall buildings. Many bamboo species flower only once every few decades. Strangely, all plants of the same species often flower at the same time, even in different countries, and then die. Scientists still do not fully understand how they coordinate this.

sach.title: The Rosetta Stone
sach.text: For centuries, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. That changed thanks to a broken slab of dark stone found in 1799 near the town of Rashid, known to Europeans as Rosetta. French soldiers discovered it while rebuilding a fort. The stone carries the same official decree written three times: in hieroglyphs, in a later Egyptian script called Demotic, and in ancient Greek. Because scholars could still read Greek, the stone offered a key to the other two scripts. Many people worked on the puzzle, but the decisive breakthrough came from the French scholar Jean-François Champollion in 1822. He realised that hieroglyphs were not just pictures of ideas but could also represent sounds. The Rosetta Stone is now kept in the British Museum in London, where it is one of the most visited objects.

sach.title: Coral Reefs
sach.text: Coral reefs look like colourful underwater gardens, but corals are actually animals. Each coral is made of tiny creatures called polyps, which build hard skeletons of limestone. Over thousands of years, these skeletons pile up and form reefs. The Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Australia is the largest reef system on Earth. Inside most corals live microscopic algae. The algae produce food from sunlight and share it with the coral, which gives them a safe home in return. This partnership also gives corals much of their colour. When the water becomes too warm for too long, corals push the algae out and turn white, a process known as bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead yet, but if the heat continues, they may starve. Although reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, they are home to about a quarter of all marine species.

news.title: Coastal Town Tests Tidal Power
news.text: Port Arden. A small coastal town in the north will begin testing tidal energy this spring. The council announced on Monday that two underwater turbines will be installed at the mouth of the harbour, where strong currents flow in and out twice a day. Together, the turbines are expected to supply electricity for around 400 homes. Unlike wind or solar power, tides are highly predictable, which makes it easier to plan when energy will be available. Local fishermen raised concerns about the effect on fish and boat traffic, so the project will be monitored by marine biologists from a nearby university for the first two years. The trial costs about 3.5 million pounds and is mostly funded by a national clean-energy programme. If the results are positive, the town hopes to add more turbines by the end of the decade.

news.title: Library Starts Lending Tools
news.text: Millbrook. Residents of Millbrook can now borrow drills, ladders and sewing machines as easily as books. The town library opened its new Library of Things on Saturday, offering more than 150 household items for free. Members can borrow up to three items at a time for one week. The idea came from a group of volunteers who noticed that many people buy tools they use only once or twice. Among the most popular items on the first day were a carpet cleaner, a tent and a karaoke machine. The project was funded by a local building company, which donated 12,000 pounds. Head librarian Sarah Okoye said the library wanted to become a place for doing, not just reading. Volunteers will also run monthly repair workshops, starting next month with a session on fixing bicycles.

news.title: Rare Bird Returns to Marsh
news.text: Kestrel Marsh. A rare bird has returned to breed in Kestrel Marsh for the first time in more than forty years. Wildlife wardens confirmed on Tuesday that a pair of bitterns has built a nest in the reed beds. The bittern, a shy brown heron known for its deep, booming call, disappeared from the area after much of the marsh was drained for farmland. Ten years ago, a conservation charity bought the land and began restoring the wetland by blocking drains and planting reeds. Warden Tom Ellis said the first booming call was heard in March by a volunteer walking her dog. To avoid disturbing the birds, part of the footpath will be closed until the end of July. Visitors are asked to stay on marked trails and keep dogs on a lead.

news.title: City Tests Car-Free Sundays
news.text: Harbourton. The centre of Harbourton will be closed to cars on the first Sunday of every month from May to September, the city council has decided. The trial follows a single car-free day last summer, which attracted around 20,000 visitors to the old town. During the closures, streets will be open only to pedestrians, cyclists and emergency vehicles. Buses will be diverted around the centre, and two park-and-ride sites will offer free parking on the edge of town. Shop owners were divided. Some reported higher sales during last year's event, while others worry that older customers will struggle to reach them. The council plans to survey residents and businesses in October before deciding whether to make the scheme permanent.

news.title: Student Builds Beach Cleaner
news.text: Seabridge. A sixteen-year-old student from Seabridge has won a national science prize for a machine that removes tiny pieces of plastic from sand. Maya Patel built the device in her garage using an old washing machine motor and a set of fine metal sieves. The machine shakes the sand so that heavier grains fall through while lighter plastic particles are collected in a container. In tests on the town's main beach, it removed up to ninety percent of visible microplastics from each sample. Maya said she started the project after a school trip where she noticed coloured specks in the sand. Her prize includes 5,000 pounds and a visit to a university laboratory. The local council has offered to test a larger version of the machine next summer.

news.title: Bakery Turns Leftover Bread into Beer
news.text: Linton. A family bakery in Linton has found a new way to deal with unsold bread. Instead of throwing it away, Hartley's Bakery now gives its leftover loaves to a local brewery, which turns them into beer. The bakery estimates that around 60 loaves were wasted every week before the partnership began. The brewery replaces part of the barley in its recipe with dried bread, and the first batch of the new ale sold out within three days. Owner James Hartley said customers had often asked what happened to bread that was not sold. Anything the brewery cannot use is given to a nearby food bank. Part of the money from every bottle sold goes to a charity that teaches cooking skills to young people.

news.title: Hills Named Dark Sky Park
news.text: Dunmoor. The hills around Dunmoor have been recognised as an official Dark Sky Park, making them one of the best places in the country to see the stars. The award follows five years of work by local residents, who persuaded farms, businesses and the council to replace bright outdoor lights with shielded lamps that point downwards. On clear nights, visitors can now see the Milky Way with the naked eye. A small observatory with two telescopes will open next spring near the village hall, run by volunteers from an amateur astronomy club. Local hotels hope the status will attract visitors in the quieter winter months, when the nights are longest. The council has also introduced rules to keep new street lighting dim and warm in colour.

news.title: Therapy Dogs Visit Hospital
news.text: Westfield. Patients at Westfield General Hospital are getting some four-legged visitors. Since January, five specially trained dogs have been visiting the children's ward and the rehabilitation unit twice a week. The dogs and their owners, all volunteers, completed a six-month training course before starting. Staff say the visits help patients relax and make difficult days easier. Nurse Linda Brooks said one young patient who had refused to walk after an operation took her first steps to stroke a golden retriever named Biscuit. Strict hygiene rules apply: the dogs are washed before every visit and do not enter intensive care. The hospital now hopes to expand the programme to its unit for older patients and is looking for more volunteers with calm, friendly dogs.

news.title: Old Railway Becomes Trail
news.text: Ashdale Valley. A disused railway line in the Ashdale Valley has reopened as a walking and cycling path. The 14-mile trail follows the route of a railway that closed in 1965 and passes through two restored tunnels and over a Victorian viaduct. The longest tunnel, almost half a mile long, has been fitted with lighting and plays recorded sounds of steam trains as people pass through. The project took four years and cost 7 million pounds, shared between the national government and three local councils. Organisers expect around 200,000 visits a year. Several cafés along the route have already reported busier weekends. The trail is fully accessible for wheelchairs and pushchairs, and bikes can be hired at both ends.

news.title: Language Café Brings People Together
news.text: Riverside. Every Thursday evening, the Riverside community centre turns into a busy café where people speak more than a dozen languages. The Language Café, started by two retired teachers, brings together newcomers learning English and local residents who want to practise Spanish, Arabic, Polish or other languages. Each table has a small flag showing which language is spoken there, and participants change tables every twenty minutes. Around 70 people now attend each week, compared with eight at the first meeting two years ago. Tea and biscuits are free, paid for by donations. Organiser Peter Walsh said the friendships formed are just as important as the language practice. Several participants have helped each other find jobs or flats. The café is now looking for a larger room.

fiction.title: The Note in the Library Book
fiction.text: Maya found the note on page forty-two, folded twice and tucked against the spine. The book was a battered guide to birds, due back in a week, and she had only borrowed it because the cover showed a heron. The note was written in pencil: ‘If you are reading this, look out of the window on the third floor at seven in the morning.’ There was no name and no date. For two days she told herself it was a joke. On the third morning she climbed the library stairs before her shift at the bakery. At seven exactly, a heron landed on the roof of the building opposite, stood still for a minute, and flew away toward the river. Maya laughed out loud. That evening she wrote her own note, folded it twice, and slipped it into a book about the stars.

fiction.title: The Yellow Umbrella
fiction.text: It had been raining for three days when Arthur found the umbrella on the bus. It was bright yellow, with a wooden handle carved in the shape of a duck. A small tag hung from the handle: ‘If found, please return to Lily, aged 7.’ There was an address on the other side. Arthur was on his way to an important meeting, and he was already late. He looked at the umbrella, then at the address, which was four stops in the wrong direction. He got off at the next stop, crossed the road and caught the bus going back. A woman opened the door of a small terraced house, and behind her a girl in pyjamas burst into tears of joy. Arthur missed his meeting. It was moved to the following week, and nobody remembered it afterwards. He still remembered the duck.
gist: A man returns a lost umbrella to a child instead of going to a meeting

fiction.title: The Last Customer
fiction.text: At five minutes to closing time, an old man walked into the shoe repair shop with a pair of brown leather boots. Daniel was tired and wanted to go home, but he took the boots anyway. The soles were worn through, and the leather was cracked. ‘They were my father's,’ the man said. ‘He wore them when he came to this country. I want my grandson to have them.’ Daniel turned the boots over in his hands. A proper repair would take hours and would cost more than a new pair. He told the man to come back on Friday. That night, he stayed until midnight, stitching and polishing. On Friday, the old man held the boots for a long time without speaking. When he asked about the price, Daniel said it had already been paid, long ago, by someone who had walked a very long way in them.

fiction.title: Snow Day
fiction.text: When the school called to say it was closed because of snow, Sam's mother had to go to work anyway, so Sam spent the day with his grandfather. Grandpa Joe was seventy-eight and moved slowly, and Sam expected a boring day of television. Instead, Grandpa took two old wooden sledges out of the garage and walked him to the steepest hill in the park. ‘I haven't done this since 1969,’ he said, and before Sam could stop him, he was racing down the slope, shouting like a teenager. He crashed into a snowdrift at the bottom and lay there laughing. They went down again and again until their gloves were soaked. On the way home, they stopped for hot chocolate, and Grandpa told stories Sam had never heard before. That evening, Sam's mother asked if he had been bored. Sam just smiled and said, ‘Can it snow again tomorrow?’

fiction.title: The Painter on the Bridge
fiction.text: Every morning, an old woman set up an easel on the stone bridge and painted the river. She painted it in fog, in sunshine, in rain and once even in a snowstorm. People hurried past on their way to work, and few stopped to look. Nadia, who crossed the bridge every day to reach her office, began to slow down and glance at the canvas. One day the woman was not there. Nor the next. After a week, Nadia asked at the café at the end of the bridge. The owner handed her an envelope. ‘She said to give this to the girl in the green coat,’ he explained. Inside was a small painting of the bridge at dawn, with a figure in a green coat in the middle, walking slowly. On the back was written: ‘Thank you for looking.’

fiction.title: Wrong Number
fiction.text: The phone rang at 2 a.m., and a voice Eliza did not know said, ‘Mum, I passed! I actually passed!’ Eliza was about to say it was a wrong number, but the young man sounded so happy that she hesitated. He explained that he had failed his nursing exam twice and had almost given up. Tonight the results had finally come out. ‘I'm so proud of you,’ Eliza said, and she meant it. They talked for ten minutes about his plans before he realised his mistake. He was horrified and apologised again and again. Eliza laughed and told him not to worry. A week later, a card arrived with no return address. It said: ‘Thank you for being my mum for ten minutes. My real one cried when I told her the next morning.’ Eliza put the card on her fridge, where it stayed for many years.

fiction.title: The Garden Gnome
fiction.text: When Mr Fischer moved into the house on Elm Road, he found a garden gnome by the front door. It was ugly, with a chipped nose and a faded red hat, so he put it in the bin. The next morning, it was back by the door. He assumed the neighbours were playing a joke and threw it away again. Again it returned. On the third morning, he hid behind the curtain and waited. At six o'clock, a small girl crept up the path, carefully placed the gnome by the door and ran away. Later he learned from the neighbours that the house had belonged to her grandmother, who had died in the spring. The gnome had always stood there. Mr Fischer glued the nose back on and painted the hat bright red again, and the next time the girl walked past, he waved.

fiction.title: Melon Bread
fiction.text: On her first day in Tokyo, Clara lost her phone and with it her map, her translation app and the address of her hotel. All she remembered was that the hotel was near a temple and a bakery that sold melon bread. She walked for an hour, getting more and more nervous. Finally she stopped an elderly man and drew a temple and a loaf of bread on a scrap of paper. He studied it seriously, nodded and set off, waving for her to follow. They walked for twenty minutes without sharing a single word of the same language. When they reached a small bakery next to a red temple gate, Clara cried out in relief. Her hotel was across the street. The man bowed, bought two pieces of melon bread, handed one to her and walked away before she could thank him properly.
gist: A stranger helps a lost tourist find her hotel without words
A tourist opens a bakery in Tokyo
An old man loses his way in a big city
q: What did she draw on the paper?

fiction.title: Second Place
fiction.text: For three years, Leo had trained for the regional piano competition, and for three years he had come second, always behind the same girl, Amara. This year he practised harder than ever. On the day of the competition, he played the best he ever had. Then Amara walked on stage, sat down, and froze. Her hands hovered above the keys, but nothing happened. The hall was silent. Leo, sitting in the front row, saw her looking at him. Without thinking, he nodded and mouthed the first notes of her piece, the way he had heard her play it in the corridor so many times. Amara took a breath and began. She played beautifully. She won, and Leo came second again. Afterwards she found him by the door. ‘You could have won,’ she said. Leo shrugged. ‘Next year,’ he said, and they both laughed.
gist: A pianist helps his rival through a moment of stage fright
A boy finally wins a piano competition

fiction.title: The Message in the Wall
fiction.text: While renovating the kitchen of their old house, Ruth and her husband found a glass bottle hidden inside the wall. In it was a letter, written in careful handwriting and dated 1952. It came from the builder, a man named Walter Green. He wrote that he hoped the family who lived here would be happy, that he had used the best timber he could afford, and that a loaf of bread cost eight pence. He added that his wife had just had a baby boy called Michael. Ruth searched online and found a Michael Green, aged seventy-three, living only two towns away. She sent him a copy of the letter. A week later, an old man stood at her door with tears in his eyes. He had never known his father, who had died when he was two. Now, for the first time, he had heard his voice.

sq3r.title: How Bridges Carry Weight

sections.p: Every bridge has to deal with two main forces. Compression pushes material together, while tension pulls it apart. A good design moves these forces safely to the ground. Engineers choose materials to match: stone and concrete are strong under compression, while steel cables cope well with tension.

An arch turns the weight above it into compression. The load travels along the curve and down into the supports at each end, called abutments. Because stone is so good at resisting compression, the Romans could build arch bridges that are still standing after almost two thousand years. The main limit of an arch is its span: very wide gaps need very tall arches.

For the longest spans, engineers use suspension bridges. The road deck hangs from vertical cables, which are attached to two main cables running over tall towers. These main cables are in tension and are anchored firmly into the ground at both ends. This design allows spans of more than two kilometres, but the deck must be stiffened so that wind does not make it swing.

yes: Some Roman arch bridges are still standing today
The main cables of a suspension bridge are in tension
no: Arch bridges are best for the widest spans
Suspension bridges do not need towers

sq3r.title: How Plants Make Their Food

sections.p: Plants do not eat in the way animals do. Instead, they make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. It takes place mainly in the leaves, inside tiny structures called chloroplasts. These contain a green pigment, chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight. Chlorophyll takes in mostly red and blue light and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green to us.

Photosynthesis needs three ingredients: light, water and carbon dioxide. Water travels up from the roots, while carbon dioxide enters through small openings in the leaves called stomata. Using the energy from light, the plant combines them into glucose, a type of sugar. Oxygen is released as a by-product. Almost all the oxygen we breathe was produced this way, by plants and by tiny algae in the oceans.

The plant uses glucose as fuel for growing and as a building material. Some of it is turned into starch and stored in roots, seeds or tubers, such as potatoes. Some is used to make cellulose, which strengthens cell walls. When we eat plants, or animals that have eaten plants, we take in energy that originally came from the Sun.

sq3r.title: The Water Cycle

sections.p: The water on Earth is constantly on the move. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes and rivers, and some of the water turns into invisible water vapour. This is called evaporation. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves, a process known as transpiration. Most of the water vapour in the air comes from the oceans, which cover about seventy percent of the Earth's surface.

As warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much vapour, so the water condenses into tiny droplets around specks of dust. Billions of these droplets form clouds. When the droplets join together and become too heavy, they fall as rain. If the air is cold enough, they fall as snow or hail instead. Together, these forms are called precipitation.

Some precipitation flows over the ground into streams and rivers and eventually returns to the sea. Some soaks into the soil and becomes groundwater, which can stay underground for thousands of years. Snow may be stored in glaciers for even longer. The total amount of water on Earth stays almost the same, so the water you drink today may once have fallen as rain on dinosaurs.
